advance.description: true: the in_progress step is done and the next pending step starts (the cheap, usual update).

done.description: 1-based numbers of steps just completed (out-of-order updates).

start.description: 1-based number of the step now in progress (with done, for out-of-order updates).

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Exit code 1
# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.
- When wiring user config into a new path, test it with a broken config too. A user rule that silently fails to load leaks the same way as one that was never wired.
- Make a fail-closed check fire only on the failure it guards against, not on a whole class of errors. A refusal on any settings error blocks unrelated cases and pushes users toward a less safe escape hatch, such as an unredacted `--raw` bundle.
- Read the Trail's current description and resolved findings before drafting review comments. The trail description can be newer than the PR description and may already list known follow-ups, which turns "you missed this" into a question about scale or timing.
- When a PR claims corpus validation, check what the corpus contained, and test on inputs from outside it, such as other languages and other codebases. A corpus drawn from one codebase can pass while common idioms elsewhere break.

# cli Review Lessons

- When replacing a git subprocess with a filesystem parser, check that it still works in bare repos and still respects exported `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`; git handles cases a parser misses.
-----
# Agent Memory

How I like agents to work, in every repo and tool. One line per preference,
with its reason. Facts about a single repo stay in that repo's memory.

- Show me the exact text before saving, changing, or deleting any memory, here
  or in a repo's memory. I want to approve anything persisted on my behalf.
- In code comments, state only what you verified. Check claims about external
  tools against their current docs, not older comments, and reference a
  constant instead of copying its value. A wrong default in a comment once hid
  a 10x timeout cut from review.
- Treat Review Lessons as guidance. Cite one only when it clearly fits the
  diff, and offer it as an option, not a requirement.
- On public threads, write in lowercase, first person, casual but precise, and
  never blame anyone. Keep review comments soft: frame points as questions or
  suggestions, say what I tried, and leave room for context I might be missing.
  Keep review comments short and straightforward: no thanks or pleasantries,
  just the point, the evidence, and one suggestion.

content.content:
### Persistent-ref CAS must preserve safety, liveness, and fairness

Persistent-ref updates need truthful error categories and lock behavior that preserves data safety without aborting pushes or starving writers.

Entire’s persistent-ref update has two lock layers: an Entire flock coordinates expensive Entire writers, while Git’s prepared ref transaction provides cross-process atomicity. A CAS conflict proves the ref moved; lock contention proves only temporary unavailability.

The two-second OPF lock timeout preserved data safety but aborted the user’s push, while polling every cancelable flock sacrificed kernel queue fairness. The corrected design lets deadline-free OPF CAS wait, restores queued locking, and tests cleanup by performing another real ref update after cancellation.

Sources: `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent_ref_update.go:93`, `cmd/entire/cli/internal/flock/flock_unix.go:72`, `cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/ref_cas_test.go:128`.
-----
### Unknown, absent, and skipped are different states

Entire must classify filesystem and configuration states positively instead of collapsing errors into absence or success.

Only a not-exist error means absent.

Unreadable, invalid, outdated, unresolved, and unsupported require different behavior and remedies.

A skipped operation is not successful when it leaves no requested target working.

User-facing output must describe the state the code actually proved.

Sources: `PR-REVIEW-RETROSPECTIVE.md`, `PR-SELF-REVIEW-CHECKLIST.md`, `GitHub PR #2052`, `August 2026 Entire CLI review corpus`.

<!-- learning-entry:8cce81414ac0 -->

### Treat automated review findings as hypotheses

Automated review comments are useful leads, but each claim must be checked against the repository's Go version, tool configuration, and runtime behavior.

Reproduce the finding before changing code.

Check the configured Go and linter versions.

Reject false findings with a command, test, or code trace.

Do not change valid Go 1.26 syntax to satisfy advice based on older language semantics.

Sources: `PR-REVIEW-RETROSPECTIVE.md`, `August 2026 Entire CLI automated review threads`.

+package session
+
+import (
+	"path/filepath"
+	"testing"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
+)
+
+func TestStateStore_Load_PreservesPendingWorkAfterExpiry(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+	cases := []struct {
+		name     string
+		state    State
+		retained bool
+	}{
+		{name: "steps", state: State{StepCount: 1}, retained: true},
+		{name: "files", state: State{FilesTouched: []string{"main.go"}}, retained: true},
+		{name: "tasks", state: State{TaskRecords: []TaskRecord{{}}}, retained: true},
+		{name: "ended-with-steps", state: State{Phase: PhaseEnded, StepCount: 1}, retained: true},
+		{name: "empty", state: State{}},
+		{name: "condensed", state: State{Phase: PhaseEnded, FullyCondensed: true}},
+	}
+	for _, tc := range cases {
+		t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			t.Parallel()
+			dir := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), SessionStateDirName)
+			store := NewStateStoreWithDir(dir)
+			tc.state.SessionID = "expired"
+			tc.state.StartedAt = time.Now().Add(-StaleSessionThreshold - 24*time.Hour)
+			require.NoError(t, store.Save(t.Context(), &tc.state))
+
+			state, err := store.Load(t.Context(), tc.state.SessionID)
+			require.NoError(t, err)
+			if tc.retained {
+				require.NotNil(t, state)
+				require.FileExists(t, filepath.Join(dir, "expired.json"))
+			} else {
+				require.Nil(t, state)
+				require.NoFileExists(t, filepath.Join(dir, "expired.json"))
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}

content.content:
Closes #2378

Related to #2350 and #2358.

Entire keeps uncondensed checkpoint commits reachable through shadow branches. Cleanup could mistake incomplete safety evidence for proof that a branch was unused: expired state with pending work could be removed, a ref read failure could be treated as absence, and malformed records could be omitted from cleanup inventory. Each path could leave shadow-only checkpoint history unreachable.

## Why cleanup could orphan history

Session state older than seven days was purged based on age even when it still recorded uncondensed checkpoint work. Separately, go-git can report an unreadable loose ref as not found, and session discovery treated that result as proof that the ref was absent. Once either state record disappeared, later cleanup saw no session protecting the shadow branch.

The cleanup inventory was also tolerant by default, so an unreadable state record could disappear from the evidence used to authorize deletion. Finally, the last protection check happened before a separate ref-deletion operation, leaving a state-change window between check and deletion.

## Make destructive decisions fail closed

State expiration now preserves records that still carry pending checkpoint content. Reference absence must be positively established; ambiguous ref errors preserve the associated state.

Ordinary session discovery remains tolerant: it logs and skips an unreadable unrelated state instead of blocking healthy session linking. Destructive paths use a strict inventory so omitted state cannot authorize deletion.

Post-push cleanup now performs its final protection check inside a prepared native Git compare-and-swap transaction. Git holds the ref lock while the guard runs, and any uncertain or failed safety check aborts before the deletion commits. Doctor and reset cleanup use the same strict-inventory boundary.

The deliberate trade-off is that uncertainty may retain stale state or a shadow branch. That is preferable to making uncondensed checkpoint history unreachable.

## Verification

`mise run check` passed on the final tree, including:

- formatting and lint
- race-enabled unit and integration tests
- 56 Vogon canaries
- 4 Roger-Roger canaries

Regression coverage includes expired uncondensed sessions, unreadable refs, malformed session state, tolerant commit linking, and guarded ref deletion on files and reftable storage.

Remove shadow branches and line attribution
-----
Remove shadow branches and line attribution
2026-10-08T20:34:37Z
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1509
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

Agent turns no longer write anything to git. Older versions committed a full working-tree snapshot to a per-worktree shadow branch (`entire/<commit>-<worktree>`) at every turn end. That was the source of runaway local storage, and cleaning those branches up at the wrong moment made uncondensed work unreachable. Turn ends now record pending work in session state only: the step count, the files the agent touched, and each touched file's git blob hash. A checkpoint is written only when you commit.

Line attribution is removed entirely, including the AI/Human/Mixed labels in `entire blame`, which now reports whether each line's commit is linked to a checkpoint. Checkpoint metadata no longer carries `initial_attribution` or `combined_attribution`; entire.io derives the experts counts from those and must be told they stop arriving.

Commits link to a session by file name: any committed path the session touched links it, except a new file at a path the agent deleted. Carry-forward after a partial commit compares the recorded hashes with the commit and the worktree, so a `git add -p` remainder, a pending deletion, or a session upgraded from the old state format keeps its uncommitted work. Gitignored files, submodule pointers, and paths inside a submodule or beneath a symlinked directory never enter the tracked files, so they can no longer keep a session pending forever; edits inside a submodule belong to the nested repository's own session. Whether a committed file still has uncommitted agent changes is asked of `git status`, so repositories with `text=auto` or `core.autocrlf` no longer keep fully committed files pending.

Lifecycle decisions (condensation, the zombie sweep, orphan cleanup, doctor) key on one predicate over session state instead of whether a shadow ref exists. Pending step rows, explain of temporary checkpoints, incremental task checkpoints and the Claude Code post-todo hook install are gone. `checkpoint list --pending` now previews what the next commit's checkpoint will contain.

Claude Code gains a transcript prompt extractor, so its prompts no longer depend on `prompt.txt` alone.

Addresses #2663, #2378, #2350, #1730, #1807 and #2653. Supersedes trail 1486 (`soph/fix-shadow-after-midturn-commit`), which patches code this PR deletes.

## Migrations

Turn ends no longer write shadow branches (entire/<commit>-<worktree>): pending work is tracked in session state and checkpoints are written only when you commit. Branches left by older versions are not removed automatically. `entire doctor` and `entire status` report them, and `entire doctor --force` or `entire disable --uninstall` deletes the `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` form without touching session state. The oldest bare `entire/<commit>` form is only ever listed, since a branch of your own named after a short SHA looks the same; `entire clean --all` removes it behind a confirmation. Do not use plain `entire clean` for this: it also clears pending session state. They hold full snapshots of your working tree, so run it once after upgrading. Deleting the branches frees no space by itself: a later `git gc` reclaims it once their objects are two weeks old. `git gc --prune=now` frees it immediately, but it drops every unreachable object in the repository (recently dropped stashes included) and must only run when no other git process is active.

`entire blame --json` reports a per-line `status` (`checkpoint`, `commit`, `uncommitted`) instead of `authorship` and `tag`. Its summary reports checkpoint-linked, commit and uncommitted line counts instead of AI/Human/Mixed counts.

New checkpoints no longer include `initial_attribution`, `combined_attribution` or `prompt_attributions`; checkpoints written by older versions keep theirs, and rewrites (explain `--generate`, attach) carry them through unchanged. Session state files written by older versions still load; their attribution and `last_checkpoint_commit_hash` keys are dropped on the next save.

The Claude Code post-todo hook is no longer installed, and any `entire enable` prunes it and says so. Its subcommand stays so older hook configs keep working. An older CLI run against the same tracked `.claude/settings.json` reports the hooks as out of date and re-adds it; this CLI removes it again on the next `entire enable`.

Commit pending agent work before downgrading to a previous release: the previous CLI deletes ended but uncondensed session state when its shadow branch is missing, and this release never writes one.

`entire session info --json` and `entire session current --json` report the number of turns not yet condensed into a checkpoint as `pending_turns`. The old `checkpoints` field is still emitted with the same value for this release only and will be removed in the next one; switch scripts to `pending_turns`. `entire status --json` adds `legacy_shadow_branches`.

## Follow-ups, not in this PR

Downgrade safety: the previous CLI deletes ended but uncondensed session state when its shadow branch is missing, and this release never writes one, so rolling back after pending work discards it. The migration note covers it; a patch on the previous release line whose orphan check also requires no pending work, named as the minimum safe downgrade target, is a release-management follow-up (trail finding 01M4DD0R83YC).

Worktree scoping, deferred to the #2531 work: scoping the zombie sweep and doctor to the current worktree, retiring the stored transcript copy with the growth check moving to the live transcript position, prompts and transcript for guest-linked commits, and capture following the event's cwd. #2531 itself must be reworked after this lands, since it pins sessions through shadow-branch steps; #2486 is expected to close in its favour.

Tracked on the priority list for go-git (#DM2KFD6): its worktree hashing lacks gitattributes, filter, and index-aware CRLF handling, which is why this PR asks `git status` instead of hashing; porting that logic into go-git would let the CLI drop the subprocess.

## Test plan

`mise run check` (fmt, lint, unit, integration, Vogon canary) and `GOOS=windows go vet ./...` on the final tree, with a cold lint cache, after merging main at `375819df95`. Every commit builds and vets on its own. A focused security review of the cross-worktree stored-transcript read (a path taken from on-disk session state, gated by `git worktree list` registration and the `.entire` anchor) found no findings. The only local failures are the known OpenCode seed-cache guard and the Claude config-probe timeout, which passes alone.

New unit, integration and command tests cover: recorded-hash carry-forward (partial commits, pending, committed and re-created deletions, upgraded sessions, an unreadable worktree); name-based linking; gitignored and submodule paths on every capture route; the doctor legacy-branch check; the `--pending` preview in text and JSON without a TTY; and the Claude prompt extractor against the real transcript fixture.

Real-agent E2E passed on `44ebccb136` for every leg (claude-code, codex, cursor-cli, copilot-cli, factoryai-droid, opencode, antigravity, roger-roger, and Windows): https://github.com/entireio/cli/actions/runs/37655720329. One changed expectation is `TestInteractiveNewFileLinksAfterUserRewrite`, which now expects a trailer after a user rewrites an agent-created file.

> **Overview**

Permanent checkpoints are written at **`git commit`** onto metadata refs, matching the updated README/CLAUDE contract.

>

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

Agent turns no longer write anything to git. Older versions committed a full working-tree snapshot to a per-worktree shadow branch (`entire/<commit>-<worktree>`) at every turn end. That was the source of runaway local storage, and cleaning those branches up at the wrong moment made uncondensed work unreachable. Turn ends now record pending work in session state only: the step count, the files the agent touched, and each touched file's git blob hash. A checkpoint is written only when you commit.

Line attribution is removed entirely, including the AI/Human/Mixed labels in `entire blame`, which now reports whether each line's commit is linked to a checkpoint. Checkpoint metadata no longer carries `initial_attribution` or `combined_attribution`; entire.io derives the experts counts from those and must be told they stop arriving.

Commits link to a session by file name: any committed path the session touched links it, except a new file at a path the agent deleted. Carry-forward after a partial commit compares the recorded hashes with the commit and the worktree, so a `git add -p` remainder, a pending deletion, or a session upgraded from the old state format keeps its uncommitted work. Gitignored files, submodule pointers, and paths inside a submodule or beneath a symlinked directory never enter the tracked files, so they can no longer keep a session pending forever; edits inside a submodule belong to the nested repository's own session. Whether a committed file still has uncommitted agent changes is asked of `git status`, so repositories with `text=auto` or `core.autocrlf` no longer keep fully committed files pending.

Lifecycle decisions (condensation, the zombie sweep, orphan cleanup, doctor) key on one predicate over session state instead of whether a shadow ref exists. Pending step rows, explain of temporary checkpoints, incremental task checkpoints and the Claude Code post-todo hook install are gone. `checkpoint list --pending` now previews what the next commit's checkpoint will contain.

Claude Code gains a transcript prompt extractor, so its prompts no longer depend on `prompt.txt` alone.

Addresses #2663, #2378, #2350, #1730, #1807 and #2653. Supersedes trail 1486 (`soph/fix-shadow-after-midturn-commit`), which patches code this PR deletes.

## Migrations

Turn ends no longer write shadow branches (entire/<commit>-<worktree>): pending work is tracked in session state and checkpoints are written only when you commit. Branches left by older versions are not removed automatically. `entire doctor` and `entire status` report them, and `entire doctor --force` or `entire disable --uninstall` deletes the `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` form without touching session state. The oldest bare `entire/<commit>` form is only ever listed, since a branch of your own named after a short SHA looks the same; `entire clean --all` removes it behind a confirmation. Do not use plain `entire clean` for this: it also clears pending session state. They hold full snapshots of your working tree, so run it once after upgrading. Deleting the branches frees no space by itself: a later `git gc` reclaims it once their objects are two weeks old. `git gc --prune=now` frees it immediately, but it drops every unreachable object in the repository (recently dropped stashes included) and must only run when no other git process is active.

`entire blame --json` reports a per-line `status` (`checkpoint`, `commit`, `uncommitted`) instead of `authorship` and `tag`. Its summary reports checkpoint-linked, commit and uncommitted line counts instead of AI/Human/Mixed counts.

New checkpoints no longer include `initial_attribution`, `combined_attribution` or `prompt_attributions`; checkpoints written by older versions keep theirs, and rewrites (explain `--generate`, attach) carry them through unchanged. Session state files written by older versions still load; their attribution and `last_checkpoint_commit_hash` keys are dropped on the next save.

The Claude Code post-todo hook is no longer installed, and any `entire enable` prunes it and says so. Its subcommand stays so older hook configs keep working. An older CLI run against the same tracked `.claude/settings.json` reports the hooks as out of date and re-adds it; this CLI removes it again on the next `entire enable`.

Commit pending agent work before downgrading to a previous release: the previous CLI deletes ended but uncondensed session state when its shadow branch is missing, and this release never writes one.

`entire session info --json` and `entire session current --json` report the number of turns not yet condensed into a checkpoint as `pending_turns`. The old `checkpoints` field is still emitted with the same value for this release only and will be removed in the next one; switch scripts to `pending_turns`. `entire status --json` adds `legacy_shadow_branches`.

## Follow-ups, not in this PR

Downgrade safety: the previous CLI deletes ended but uncondensed session state when its shadow branch is missing, and this release never writes one, so rolling back after pending work discards it. The migration note covers it; a patch on the previous release line whose orphan check also requires no pending work, named as the minimum safe downgrade target, is a release-management follow-up (trail finding 01M4DD0R83YC).

Worktree scoping, deferred to the #2531 work: scoping the zombie sweep and doctor to the current worktree, retiring the stored transcript copy with the growth check moving to the live transcript position, prompts and transcript for guest-linked commits, and capture following the event's cwd. #2531 itself must be reworked after this lands, since it pins sessions through shadow-branch steps; #2486 is expected to close in its favour.

Tracked on the priority list for go-git (#DM2KFD6): its worktree hashing lacks gitattributes, filter, and index-aware CRLF handling, which is why this PR asks `git status` instead of hashing; porting that logic into go-git would let the CLI drop the subprocess.

## Test plan

`mise run check` (fmt, lint, unit, integration, Vogon canary) and `GOOS=windows go vet ./...` on the final tree, with a cold lint cache, after merging main at `375819df95`. Every commit builds and vets on its own. A focused security review of the cross-worktree stored-transcript read (a path taken from on-disk session state, gated by `git worktree list` registration and the `.entire` anchor) found no findings. The only local failures are the known OpenCode seed-cache guard and the Claude config-probe timeout, which passes alone.

New unit, integration and command tests cover: recorded-hash carry-forward (partial commits, pending, committed and re-created deletions, upgraded sessions, an unreadable worktree); name-based linking; gitignored and submodule paths on every capture route; the doctor legacy-branch check; the `--pending` preview in text and JSON without a TTY; and the Claude prompt extractor against the real transcript fixture.

Real-agent E2E passed on `44ebccb136` for every leg (claude-code, codex, cursor-cli, copilot-cli, factoryai-droid, opencode, antigravity, roger-roger, and Windows): https://github.com/entireio/cli/actions/runs/37655720329. One changed expectation is `TestInteractiveNewFileLinksAfterUserRewrite`, which now expects a trailer after a user rewrites an agent-created file.

content.content:
Cleanup can make uncondensed checkpoint commits unreachable after state expiry or a ref read failure
OPEN  
## What happened?

Entire keeps uncondensed checkpoint commits reachable through shadow branches. Cleanup uses session state to decide whether a shadow branch still contains work that must be preserved.

Two independent bugs can delete valid session state before condensation finishes:

1. Loading session state deletes it once it is more than seven days old, even when it records pending checkpoint work.
2. Session discovery deletes state when a Git ref lookup returns `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound`, even when the ref exists but could not be read.

Both bugs produce the same failure:

1. A session has checkpoint commits that exist only on its shadow branch.
2. Entire deletes the session state that associates those commits with pending work.
3. Cleanup classifies the shadow branch as unused and deletes it.
4. The shadow-only commits become unreachable.
5. Git may eventually garbage-collect them.

This affects checkpoint history that has not yet been condensed. It does not delete working-tree files or commits already reachable from ordinary Git branches.

### Bug 1: state expiry ignores pending work

`StateStore.Load` deletes session state after seven days based only on its timestamp.

It does not check whether the state still records uncondensed work. A valid state with `FullyCondensed: false` and a non-zero `StepCount` is therefore deleted as soon as it crosses the expiry threshold.

The expiry check is destructive. Merely loading the state removes the evidence cleanup needs to protect the corresponding shadow branch.

This affects both active and ended sessions.

### Bug 2: a ref read failure is treated as proof that the ref is absent

Session discovery removes state that appears to refer to a missing shadow branch.

An existing loose ref can be unreadable because of a filesystem error or permission problem. In that case, go-git may return `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound`. Session discovery treats that result as proof that the ref does not exist and deletes the state as orphaned.

If the ref becomes readable again, its session state is already gone. The next cleanup pass sees no session protecting the branch and deletes it.

A failed lookup is not enough evidence that deleting the state is safe.

## Steps to reproduce

### State expiry

1. Create a shadow branch containing a commit that is not reachable from any ordinary branch.
2. Save valid session state for the shadow branch with `FullyCondensed: false` and `StepCount: 1`.
3. Set the session timestamps to one hour ago.
4. Run pushed-shadow cleanup.
5. Confirm that cleanup preserves the shadow branch.
6. Change only the timestamps so the state is eight days old.
7. Load the state or run the cleanup path that loads it.
8. Observe that Entire deletes both the state and the shadow branch.
9. Run `git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs`.
10. Observe that the shadow-only commit is unreachable.

Observed output:

```text
phase=active control_deleted=0 aged_deleted=1 state_deleted=true
-----
Post-push cleanup deletes an uncondensed shadow ref when its session state is malformed | OPEN null
fix(strategy): prevent shadow cleanup with malformed session state | OPEN null

Main's comment notes that IDLE states rely on StaleSessionThreshold to age out after 7 days, so the local fix of retaining stale IDLE states with pending work indefinitely is a real departure from upstream's documented design — a reviewer could reasonably ask what mechanism retires them if a user abandons a session with pending FilesTouched that never get committed.

I'm checking whether `deleteStale=false` still returns the loaded state correctly — it does, falling through to `&state` same as the original path. I also notice HasPendingWork ignores FullyCondensed, so a fully condensed, stale session with lingering TaskRecords from a late-finishing subagent would also be retained forever, which seems like an unbounded-retention edge case worth flagging.

This raises a real concern: if a task record never completes, say the agent crashed mid-subagent, TaskRecords never clears and the state never ages out, removing the old backstop. I want to check whether anything prunes FilesTouched once the worktree matches HEAD again, and whether doctor's stuck-session flow (which lets users discard) serves as the manual escape hatch here, since the PR description does acknowledge this trade-off explicitly.

Also worth checking: the FullyCondensed:true case with lingering TaskRecords is still retained under HasPendingWork, which seems like a gap worth flagging. I should look at the existing `entire status` display logic around state.go:1132 to see what else depends on stale-session deletion before concluding.

The main function still deletes expired state regardless of pending work, but now documents the 7-day age-out as the retirement path for IDLE sessions. I'll check what else depends on that before writing up findings.

======
Hooks stop deleting live idle sessions
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1413
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Hooks stop deleting live idle sessions

**Symptom.** A session is re-initialised from scratch every few turns: transcript window, owner, and home reset, and a commit landing in the gap finds no session at all. In one clone a single session was re-initialised 37 times in four days.

**Cause.** The strategy's session listing, which every hook runs to match sessions, deletes any non-active state whose shadow branch is gone and whose checkpoint ID is empty. That is the normal shape of a healthy idle session right after a linked commit, or of a read-only session. Hooks in other worktrees list the same shared store, so any of them could delete it.

**Fix.** Orphan cleanup now deletes only finalized sessions (`State.IsEnded`: ENDED phase or `EndedAt` stamped) that were never condensed and carry no task records. Unfinalized IDLE states are never deleted by the listing: a live idle session stays, and a dead-owner one is left for `finalizeExitedSessions`, which marks it ENDED so the next listing clears it. Legacy empty-phase records normalize to IDLE, so — unlike before — they are kept until the 7-day `StaleSessionThreshold` expiry. `entire status` was already fixed to not delete on read (#2363); this covers the hooks.

**Tests.** Integration: another worktree's commit hook no longer deletes an idle session. Unit: the cleanup table keeps idle-with-dead-owner, idle-with-unknown-owner and legacy-empty-phase, and deletes ENDED never-condensed and IDLE-with-`EndedAt` states.

**Follow-up.** Hooks should not delete session state at all; deletion belongs to the sweeper, doctor and the 7-day expiry. That needs the orphan filter moved out of the shared listing and is tracked

content.content:
root (both `session.NewStateStore` and `NewStateStoreForWorktree`), so a test
missing repo isolation fails loudly instead of leaking fixture sessions into
a real repo's `.git/entire-sessions` — leaked fixtures once hijacked commit
linking and produced a dangling `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.

**Background zombie sweep.** The session-start hook checks the shared
session-state directory for zombies — non-ended sessions whose owning agent
process has exited (including the common IDLE case), and ENDED sessions that
still hold uncondensed checkpoint data more than 24h after ending (younger ones
are left alone so PostCommit carry-forward keeps its chance). When any exist,
it spawns a detached
`__sweep_sessions` process (throttled to one spawn per repo per window via a
flock-serialized marker in the git common dir) that finalizes/condenses them
using the same engines as `entire doctor --force`, condense-only: the sweep
has no interactive condense deadline and never initiates a discard — ended
sessions with nothing pending (`State.HasPendingWork`) are left to `entire doctor`
(and the existing orphan cleanup). The 7-day stale-session
purge bounds the sweep's window: a zombie that stays unfixed past 7 days is
removed by the purge, not the sweep. See `cmd/entire/cli/session_sweep.go`.

### Turn-End State

A turn end (`SaveStep`) writes no git objects. It records the turn into session state and leaves the transcript on local disk:

- `StepCount` is incremented, `FilesTouched` gains the turn's modified, new and deleted paths, and `TouchedFileHashes` records the git blob hash of each modified or new regular file (hashed with `git hash-object`, so clean filters apply exactly as `git add` would) and `""` for each deleted path. A path whose hash is unknown — hashing failed, a symlink, or a path that arrived through a task record, a per-tool hook, or a Codex child-file merge (`MergeUnhashedFilesTouched`, which also drops any hash an earlier step recorded for it) — has no entry and falls back to name matching. Paths this turn named that neither exist nor are recorded deletions are dropped from `FilesTouched` as phantoms.
- The turn's paths come from the transcript analyzer plus `git status` (`DetectFileChanges`): modified and deleted tracked files, and untracked files absent from the prompt-start baseline (`PrePromptState.UntrackedFiles`). An untracked file already in that baseline counts as modified when its stat data no longer matches `PrePromptState.UntrackedFileStats`, since git status reports it as untracked either way and a shell edit leaves no trace in the transcript. The stat data is what git's index compares: size, modification time, inode and status-change time. The change time catches a same-size rewrite that restores the modification time (`cp -p`, `touch -r`); Windows exposes no change time, so only size and modification time are compared there. The stat pass runs inside `UserPromptSubmit`, so it is bounded: above 10,000 untracked files it records no stats, and it stops after 500ms with what it has. Edits to the files it left out are not detected, as with state written before stats existed.

are left alone so PostCommit carry-forward keeps its chance). When any exist,
it spawns a detached
`__sweep_sessions` process (throttled to one spawn per repo per window via a
flock-serialized marker in the git common dir) that finalizes/condenses them
using the same engines as `entire doctor --force`, condense-only: the sweep
has no interactive condense deadline and never initiates a discard — ended
sessions with nothing pending (`State.HasPendingWork`) are left to `entire doctor`
(and the existing orphan cleanup). The 7-day stale-session
purge bounds the sweep's window: a zombie that stays unfixed past 7 days is
removed by the purge, not the sweep. See `cmd/entire/cli/session_sweep.go`.

### Turn-End State

A turn end (`SaveStep`) writes no git objects. It records the turn into session state and leaves the transcript on local disk:

- `StepCount` is incremented, `FilesTouched` gains the turn's modified, new and deleted paths, and `TouchedFileHashes` records the git blob hash of each modified or new regular file (hashed with `git hash-object`, so clean filters apply exactly as `git add` would) and `""` for each deleted path. A path whose hash is unknown — hashing failed, a symlink, or a path that arrived through a task record, a per-tool hook, or a Codex child-file merge (`MergeUnhashedFilesTouched`, which also drops any hash an earlier step recorded for it) — has no entry and falls back to name matching. Paths this turn named that neither exist nor are recorded deletions are dropped from `FilesTouched` as phantoms.
- The turn's paths come from the transcript analyzer plus `git status` (`DetectFileChanges`): modified and deleted tracked files, and untracked files absent from the prompt-start baseline (`PrePromptState.UntrackedFiles`). An untracked file already in that baseline counts as modified when its stat data no longer matches `PrePromptState.UntrackedFileStats`, since git status reports it as untracked either way and a shell edit leaves no trace in the transcript. The stat data is what git's index compares: size, modification time, inode and status-change time. The change time catches a same-size rewrite that restores the modification time (`cp -p`, `touch -r`); Windows exposes no change time, so only size and modification time are compared there. The stat pass runs inside `UserPromptSubmit`, so it is bounded: above 10,000 untracked files it records no stats, and it stops after 500ms with what it has. Edits to the files it left out are not detected, as with state written before stats existed.

## Findings on the reduced (local) change
1. HasPendingWork ignores FullyCondensed. A fully condensed ENDED session with a leftover task record (doctor.go says it "can never complete") is now never purged. Nothing else removes it either: orphan cleanup needs an empty LastCheckpointID, doctor skips it, and the sweep skips it.
2. The 7-day purge is the documented bound on the zombie sweep (sessions-and-checkpoints.md "7-day stale-session purge bounds the sweep's window"). A !FullyCondensed ENDED zombie that keeps failing to condense would now re-spawn a detached sweep every 15 min, with no end. Docs and comments need updating: the StaleSessionThreshold doc, manual_commit_session.go:164, checkpoint-implementation.md:66, sessions-and-checkpoints.md:277.
3. The test checks only that the file is retained, which mirrors the predicate. It does not check that a retained stale session is still linked/condensed by a later commit (the "test the retry" lesson).
4. The published PR's predicate also kept TurnCheckpointIDs and CondensationAttempt. The local one drops them. Matching upstream's "single predicate" rule is fine, but say so in the PR.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# entireio/cli#2385 review notes (fix-session-cleanup-safety)

Read-only review, 2026-10-19. Nothing edited, committed, pushed, or posted.

## State
- Published head c164844c2 (Sep 17), base 5c277cf95. GitHub: CONFLICTING / DIRTY, REVIEW_REQUIRED (cli-maintainers), 0 reviews, 0 comments.
- Upstream #2692 (merged Oct 8, "Remove shadow branches") deleted every shadow-branch cleanup path this PR guards, and lists #2378 (this PR's issue) as addressed. #2378 is still open.
- `git merge-tree c164844c2 upstream/main` (a334cb698): conflicts in 8 files (doctor.go, ref_cas_test.go, cleanup.go, cleanup_pushed_shadow_test.go modify/delete, manual_commit_condensation.go, manual_commit_reset.go, manual_commit_session.go, checkpoint-implementation.md).
- Local, unpushed: one merge commit 7b6f9c225 (merged main ffc17a1df of Oct 14, took upstream's side). It left dead code behind: ListStrict, ListSessionStatesStrict, CompareAndSwapRefGuarded, ReferenceIsAbsent, HasShadowBranchContent, all with no production callers.
- Uncommitted: staged changes revert those 7 files to main; unstaged changes reduce the PR to a 3-file fix: `StateStore.load` keeps stale state when `HasPendingWork()`; there is a retention test table; the stale-delete fixture drops StepCount.
- HEAD plus the uncommitted diff applies cleanly on current main (a334cb698) and builds.

## CI / trail
- CI never ran: every run on all 4 pushes (Sep 11-17) failed with 0 jobs ("workflow file issue"). The same thing happened on the user's other fork PRs Sep 7-18. #2213 runs passed on Oct 14, so a new push should get real CI.
- No trail on entireio/cli. The fork trail gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli#3 (title is the #2350 wording, not linked to the PR) has 2 open medium findings. Both point at cleanup.go code that upstream deleted, and both look wrong on the code they cite.

## Findings on the reduced (local) change
1. HasPendingWork ignores FullyCondensed. A fully condensed ENDED session with a leftover task record (doctor.go says it "can never complete") is now never purged. Nothing else removes it either: orphan cleanup needs an empty LastCheckpointID, doctor skips it, and the sweep skips it.
2. The 7-day purge is the documented bound on the zombie sweep (sessions-and-checkpoints.md "7-day stale-session purge bounds the sweep's window"). A !FullyCondensed ENDED zombie that keeps failing to condense would now re-spawn a detached sweep every 15 min, with no end. Docs and comments need updating: the StaleSessionThreshold doc, manual_commit_session.go:164, checkpoint-implementation.md:66, sessions-and-checkpoints.md:277.
3. The test checks only that the file is retained, which mirrors the predicate. It does not check that a retained stale session is still linked/condensed by a later commit (the "test the retry" lesson).
4. The published PR's predicate also kept TurnCheckpointIDs and CondensationAttempt. The local one drops them. Matching upstream's "single predicate" rule is fine, but say so in the PR.

content.text:
I reviewed [entireio/cli#2385](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2385) without changing anything. Most of the published PR is obsolete: upstream [entireio/cli#2692](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2692), merged Oct 8, removed shadow branches. Your uncommitted work cuts the PR to a 3-file fix, which builds and passes its tests on current main. Notes for the sibling sessions are in `pr-2385-fix-session-cleanup-safety.md` in the shared notes folder.

## 1. Local worktree vs the published PR

- **Published head** is `c164844c2` (Sep 17): 19 files, +747/−154. GitHub says it **conflicts** with main.
- **Local-only commit (not pushed):** one merge, `7b6f9c225` "Merge upstream/main" (Oct 14). It took upstream's side for every shadow-branch path. That left dead code behind with no production callers: `ListStrict`, `ListSessionStatesStrict`, `CompareAndSwapRefGuarded`, `ReferenceIsAbsent` and `HasShadowBranchContent`.
- **Staged changes:** they put 7 files back exactly as main has them, which deletes that dead code.
- **Unstaged changes:** the PR shrinks to 3 files.
  - In `StateStore.load`, an expired session is deleted only if `!HasPendingWork()` ([state.go:1246](cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go:1246)).
  - A 45-line retention test.
  - The stale-delete test fixture no longer sets `StepCount`.
- On top of current main (`a334cb698`) this merges and applies cleanly. Build, vet, the session and gitrepo packages, and the stale/orphan/sweep strategy tests all pass. The one failure was `TestNewStateStore_RefusesRealRepoUnderGoTest`, and only because my scratch copy isn't a git repo.

## 2. Brief

**What it does for users:** today Entire deletes any session state file that has been idle for 7 days, even when it holds agent work that hasn't been checkpointed yet. Come back after a week, commit the agent's files, and the commit no longer links to a checkpoint. The local change keeps those files.

**Why it still matters:** the published PR guarded shadow-branch deletion, and #2692 deleted that code. #2692 also lists #2378, this PR's issue, as addressed, but #2378 is still open. Now that turn ends write nothing to git, the state file is the *only* record of pending work. Main's own comment on `OwnerExited` admits that the 7-day purge discards "pending checkpoint work instead of condensing it".

**Performance, compatibility, data:** no format change, and the cost is negligible. The risk is that some state files are now kept with no end date (see findings 1 and 2).

**Uncertain:** whether maintainers accept retention with no end date. #2573 says deletion belongs to "the sweeper, doctor and the 7-day expiry", and #617 treated sessions that never expire as a bug.

## Findings (on the local version)

1. **Medium: some sessions are now never deleted.** `HasPendingWork()` ignores `FullyCondensed`. A fully condensed, ended session that still has a task record is kept forever. Doctor skips it ([doctor.go:377-381](cmd/entire/cli/doctor.go:377)) and says that kind of record "can never complete". The sweep and orphan cleanup skip it too.
   - **Option:** delete an expired session when `FullyCondensed || !HasPendingWork()`.
2. **Medium: the sweep's 7-day limit disappears.** The docs say the 7-day purge bounds the zombie sweep ([sessions-and-checkpoints.md:277](docs/architecture/sessions-and-checkpoints.md:277)). A session that keeps failing to condense would now start a background sweep every 15 minutes with no end date.
   - **Needed:** keep a limit, or say why none is needed. Then update the `StaleSessionThreshold` doc comment ([state.go:30](cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go:30)), [manual_commit_session.go:164](cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_session.go:164) and [checkpoint-implementation.md:66](docs/development/checkpoint-implementation.md:66).
3. **Medium: the test doesn't prove the fix.** It checks that the file survives, which just restates the condition in the code. Your General.md lesson ("test the retry itself") applies. An integration test should age a session with pending files, commit those files, and check that the commit still gets its checkpoint.
4. **Low:** the published version also kept sessions with `TurnCheckpointIDs` or `CondensationAttempt` set. The local version drops both by switching to `HasPendingWork`. That matches upstream's single-check rule; say so in the PR.

Your cli.md lesson (the bare-repo/`GIT_DIR` check) doesn't apply here.

## 3. Review readiness

- **CI has never run.** All runs on all 4 pushes failed with 0 jobs ("workflow file issue"). Your other fork PRs hit the same thing Sep 7-18, and #2213 ran fine on Oct 14, so a new push should get real CI.
- **Reviews:** none, and no comments. It's waiting on cli-maintainers.
- **Mergeability:** conflicts in 8 files, one of them a file main deleted that this PR modifies.
- **Trail:** there is none on entireio/cli. The fork has trail [gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli#3](https://entire.io/gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli/trails/3), which isn't linked to the PR and is titled after #2350. Its 2 open medium findings both point at `cleanup.go` code upstream deleted, and both look wrong anyway.
- **PR body:** it describes code that no longer exists.

## Recommended next steps

1. Fix findings 1-3 on the local change. I'd give you a pre-edit brief first.
2. Commit the staged and unstaged work, and push to the existing PR to replace the published head.
3. Rewrite the PR title and description to cover only the stale-state fix.
4. Create a Trail on entireio/cli and link it.
5. Ask whether [entireio/cli#2378](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2378) Bug 2 and [entireio/cli#2350](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2350) can be closed as fixed by #2692.

The other option is to close #2385 in favour of a fresh, focused PR. I'll wait for your go-ahead either way.
